claim: The unc-2(zf35gf) mutation is a single-base transition (GGA to AGA) in the 17th exon of unc-2.
source: Sequencing analysis of the zf35 allele revealed a single-base transition (GGAto AGA) in the 17th exon of unc-2 (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the molecular nature of the mutation based on sequencing analysis.

claim: The zf35 mutation results in a glycine to arginine substitution (G1132R) in UNC-2/CaV2α.
source: The zf35 mutation results in a glycine to arginine substitution (G1132R) in the highly conserved intracellular linker between III-S6 and IV-S1 (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the amino acid change resulting from the mutation.

claim: unc-2(zf35gf) mutants exhibit hyperactive locomotion with increased reversal frequency compared to wild type.
source: This clonic seizure-like phenotype of zf35 mutants was accompanied by an increased locomotion rate during bouts of forward or backward locomotion. On average, zf35 mutants moved approximately 1.5 fold faster than wild-type animals (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The manuscript presents behavioral data showing increased locomotion rate in mutants.

claim: unc-2(zf35gf) mutants have a reversal frequency of 43.1 ± 2.0 per 3 minutes compared to 6.8 ± 0.4 per 3 minutes in wild type.
source: reversal frequency: zf35: 43.1 ± 2.0/3 min, n = 59; wild type: 6.8 ± 0.4/3 min, n = 59) (Figure 1; Video 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements of reversal frequency.

claim: The zf35 mutation is semi-dominant.
source: Animals heterozygous for the zf35 mutation also displayed increased velocity and reversal frequency (Figure 1A–C), albeit to a lesser extent when compared to homozygous mutants. This indicates that the zf35 mutation is semi-dominant.
evidence: The manuscript presents data on heterozygous animals and explicitly states the semi-dominant nature.

claim: unc-2(zf35gf) mutants are smaller than wild-type animals.
source: zf35 mutant animals were slightly smaller than wild-type animals (0.82 ± 0.03 mm, n = 75 vs 1.00 ± 0.04 mm, n = 88) (Figure 1D)
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative measurements of animal size.

claim: unc-2(zf35gf) mutants have reduced brood size compared to wild type.
source: had a reduced brood size (wild type: 207 ± 11, n = 5, zf35: 150 ± 16, n = 5).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative measurements of brood size.

claim: unc-2(zf35gf) mutants retain fewer eggs in the uterus than wild-type animals.
source: Furthermore, zf35 adults retained a reduced number of eggs in the uterus (zf35: 3.6 ± 0.2, n = 86; wild type: 14.1 ± 0.6, n = 80) (Figure 1E).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative measurements of egg retention.

claim: unc-2(zf35gf) mutants lay eggs at an earlier developmental stage than wild-type animals.
source: zf35 mutants laid eggs that are at an earlier developmental stage than wild-type animals, indicating that the time between fertilization and egg laying was reduced (Figure 1F).
evidence: The manuscript presents data on developmental stages of laid eggs.

claim: Pan-neuronal expression of the unc-2(zf35) transgene induces hyperactive behavior in both wild-type and unc-2 loss-of-function mutant backgrounds.
source: Pan-neuronal expression of the unc-2(zf35) transgene, in both wild-type and unc-2 loss-of-function mutant (lf) backgrounds, induced hyperactive behavior similar to that of the zf35 mutant.
evidence: The manuscript describes transgenic rescue experiments demonstrating sufficiency of the mutation.

claim: Transgenic overexpression of wild-type unc-2 cDNA does not induce hyperactive behavior.
source: Transgenic overexpression of the wild-type unc-2 cDNA rescued the uncoordinated and lethargic phenotype of unc-2(lf) mutants, but did not induce hyperactive behavior (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript presents control experiments with wild-type transgene.

claim: UNC-2(G1132R)::GFP localizes to cell soma and puncta along neuronal processes similar to wild-type UNC-2::GFP.
source: UNC-2(GF/G1132R)::GFP was observed in the cell soma, and in puncta along the neuronal processes (Figure 2D). The fluorescence expression pattern of UNC-2(GF/G1132R)::GFP animals displayed no obvious difference with that of a UNC-2(WT)::GFP transgene (Figure 2D) (Saheki and Bargmann, 2009).
evidence: The manuscript describes fluorescence microscopy observations comparing mutant and wild-type protein localization.

claim: UNC-2(G1132R) is properly processed and trafficked to presynaptic sites.
source: This indicates that UNC-2(G1132R) is properly processed and trafficked to presynaptic sites.
evidence: The manuscript infers proper trafficking from the localization data.

claim: Seven intragenic suppressor alleles of unc-2(zf35gf) harbor missense or non-sense secondary mutations in the unc-2 gene.
source: From a screen of mutagenized unc-2(zf35) mutants, we identified seven intragenic suppressor alleles that harbor missense or non-sense secondary mutations in the unc-2 gene (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript describes a genetic screen and sequencing results.

claim: Four intragenic suppressors (zf109, zf113, zf115, and zf124) revert the zf35 hyperactivity phenotype to sluggish locomotion similar to unc-2(e55) loss-of-function.
source: Four suppressors, zf109, zf113, zf115 and zf124 reverted the zf35 hyperactivity phenotype to sluggish locomotion, similar to the canonical loss-of-function unc-2(e55) allele (Figure 2F).
evidence: The manuscript presents behavioral data on suppressor mutants.

claim: The zf113(W550stop) and zf124(M1369stop) alleles result in premature stop codons and likely represent null alleles of unc-2.
source: The zf113(W550stop) and zf124(M1369stop) alleles result in premature stop codons and therefore likely represent null alleles of unc-2.
evidence: The manuscript identifies nonsense mutations and infers their null nature.

claim: The ability of intragenic suppressors to revert the hyperactive phenotype strongly suggests that zf35 is a gain-of-function allele of unc-2.
source: Their ability to revert the hyperactive phenotype of zf35 mutants to that of the wild-type or unc-2(lf) mutants strongly suggest that the zf35 mutation is a gain-of-function allele of unc-2.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the suppressor analysis.

claim: The CACNA1A(G1518R) CaV2.1α channel exhibits a −10 mV shift in activation potential compared to wild-type.
source: Whole-cell patch clamp experiments (Figure 3A) showed that the CACNA1A(G1518R) CaV2.1α channel exhibited a −10 mV shift in activation potential when compared to the wild-type CaV2.1α channel (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data from patch clamp experiments.

claim: The maximal current density of G1518R channels is 1.7-fold larger than wild type.
source: The maximal current density was 1.7-fold larger for G1518R channels (80.6 ± 5.7 pA/pF, n = 11) compared to wild type (47.5 ± 4.3 pA/pF, n = 13) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The slope of the activation curve is not significantly affected in the CACNA1A(G1518R) channel.
source: The slope of the activation curve was not significantly affected in the CACNA1A(G1518R) channel (KaWT = 3.8 ± 0.2 mV; Ka G1518R = 4.1 ± 0.1 mV, Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative analysis of activation kinetics.

claim: Wild-type and G1518R CaV2.1 channels decay with similar mono-exponential time courses.
source: Both wild-type and G1518R CaV2.1 channels decayed with similar mono-exponential time courses (Tinac CACNA1A(wt)=177 ± 45 ms and Tinac CACNA1A(G1518R)=196 ± 32 ms at a 0 mV pulse).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative measurements of channel inactivation kinetics.

claim: The transition from open to inactive states is not affected by the G1518R mutation.
source: This suggests that the transition from the open to the inactive states was not affected by the G1518R mutation.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the similar decay time courses.

claim: The G1518R channels exhibit a 7.7 mV shift to more positive potentials in steady-state inactivation compared to wild type.
source: The membrane potential at which half of the current was inactivated in the G1518R channels exhibited a 7.7 mV shift to more positive potentials compared to wild type (V0.5inact= -55.0 ± 1.0 mV and −47.3 ± 1.0 mV for the wild-type and G1518R channels, respectively).
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative measurements of steady-state inactivation.

claim: The G1518R mutation leads to channels that are activated at lower membrane potentials and inactivated at higher membrane potentials.
source: Thus, the G1518R mutation leads to channels that are activated at lower membrane potentials, and inactivated at higher membrane potentials.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the electrophysiological findings.

claim: The G1518R mutation increases current density by CACNA1A(G1518R).
source: Together, these properties lead to increased current density by CACNA1A(G1518R).
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the combined electrophysiological data.

claim: Pan-neuronal expression of unc-2(R192Q) or unc-2(S218L) transgenes results in phenotypes similar to unc-2(zf35gf) mutants.
source: Pan-neuronal expression of the unc-2(R192Q) or unc-2(S218L) transgene in C. elegans resulted in phenotypes similar to unc-2(zf35gf) mutants.
evidence: The manuscript describes transgenic experiments with FHM1 mutations.

claim: unc-2(R192Q) animals exhibit increased reversal frequency of 25.5/min ±0.9 compared to wild-type animals at 4.2/min ±0.5.
source: Specifically, both unc-2(R192Q) and unc-2(S218L) animals exhibited increased reversal frequencies (25.5/min ±0.9, n = 34 and 16.5/min ±0.9, n = 33, respectively) when compared to wild-type animals (4.2/min ±0.5, n = 29) (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative behavioral measurements.

claim: unc-2(FHM1) transgenic animals display hyperactive egg-laying behavior.
source: They also displayed hyperactive egg-laying behavior (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript describes egg-laying phenotypes of FHM1 transgenic animals.

claim: unc-2(R192Q) animals retain 5.7 ± 0.4 eggs in the uterus compared to 16.5 ± 0.8 in wild-type animals.
source: unc-2(FHM1) transgenic animals laid eggs that are at an earlier developmental stage and retained fewer eggs in the uterus (unc-2(R192Q): 5.7 ± 0.4, n = 37; unc-2(S218L): 8.4 ± 0.6, n = 32, respectively), when compared to wild-type animals (16.5 ± 0.8, n = 23).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative measurements of egg retention.

claim: FHM1 mutations are gain-of-function mutations that lead to increased CaV2 activity.
source: These experiments provide strong genetic evidence that, similar to unc-2(zf35), the FHM1 mutations are gain-of-function mutations that lead to increased CaV2 activity.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the FHM1 transgenic experiments.

claim: unc-2(zf35gf) mutants are hypersensitive to aldicarb, with almost 100% paralyzed within 30 minutes.
source: In sharp contrast, almost 100% of unc-2(zf35gf) mutants became paralyzed within 30 min (Figure 4D).
evidence: The manuscript presents pharmacological assay data.

claim: Approximately 50% of wild-type animals exposed to 1 mM aldicarb became paralyzed within 1 hour.
source: Approximately 50% of wild-type animals exposed to 1 mM aldicarb became paralyzed within 1 hr, consistent with previous findings (Miller et al., 1996; Mathews et al., 2003)
evidence: The manuscript presents pharmacological data and cites previous studies.

claim: Less than 15% of unc-2(lf) mutants were paralyzed within 1 hour on aldicarb.
source: while less than 15% unc-2(lf) mutants were paralyzed within 1 hr (Figure 4D).
evidence: The manuscript presents pharmacological assay data.

claim: Pan-neuronal expression of unc-2(R192Q) or unc-2(S218L) induced hypersensitivity to aldicarb.
source: Pan-neuronal expression of unc-2(R192Q) or unc-2(S218L) also induced hypersensitivity to aldicarb (Figure 4E).
evidence: The manuscript presents pharmacological data on FHM1 transgenic animals.

claim: Hypersensitivity to aldicarb in FHM1 transgenic animals is not due to overexpression of the unc-2 transgene.
source: This hypersensitivity is not due to overexpression of the unc-2 transgene because expression of a wild-type unc-2 transgene, which restored the locomotion defects in unc-2(lf) mutants, led to wild-type sensitivity to aldicarb (Figure 4E).
evidence: The manuscript presents control experiments to rule out overexpression effects.

claim: Animals with gain-of-function mutations in unc-2/CaV2α are hypersensitive to aldicarb, which may reflect increased ACh release at the neuromuscular junction.
source: Therefore, animals with gain-of-function mutations in unc-2/CaV2α are hypersensitive to aldicarb, which may reflect increased ACh release at the neuromuscular junction (NMJ).
evidence: The manuscript interprets the aldicarb hypersensitivity data.

claim: unc-2(zf35gf) mutants show an over two-fold increase in the overall frequency of spontaneous PSCs compared to wild-type animals.
source: unc-2(zf35gf) mutants showed an over two-fold increase in the overall frequency of spontaneous PSCs when compared to wild-type animals (Figure 5A and B)
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological recordings from body wall muscles.

claim: unc-2(zf35gf) mutants show no significant changes in the mean amplitude of spontaneous PSCs.
source: with no significant changes in the mean amplitude (Figure 5A and C).
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data on PSC amplitude.

claim: The frequency of spontaneous EPSCs was increased by approximately 1.5-fold in unc-2(zf35gf); unc-49 double mutants compared with control unc-49 single mutants.
source: The frequency of spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) was increased by approximately 1.5-fold in unc-2(zf35gf); unc-49 double mutants compared with control unc-49 single mutants (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological recordings isolating cholinergic currents.

claim: The frequency of spontaneous IPSC was reduced by half in unc-2(zf35gf) mutants without significant changes in amplitude.
source: The frequency of spontaneous IPSC was reduced by half, without significant changes in the amplitude (Figure 5G–I).
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological recordings isolating GABAergic currents.

claim: The UNC-2/CaV2α(GF) mutation differentially affects excitatory and inhibitory signaling, shifting the E/I balance toward excitatory transmission.
source: Our data show that, despite being expressed by both cholinergic and GABAergic motor neurons, the unc-2(zf35gf) mutation leads to increased cholinergic and decreased GABAergic transmission to body wall muscles. Thus, instead of causing a uniform increase of neural signaling, the UNC-2/CaV2α(GF) mutation differentially affects excitatory and inhibitory signaling, shifting the E/I balance toward excitatory transmission.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the electrophysiological findings and draws a conclusion.

claim: RAB-3::mCherry puncta are larger in unc-2(zf35gf) mutants at cholinergic NMJs.
source: RAB-3::mCherry puncta were larger in unc-2(zf35gf) mutants (Figure 6A and B)
evidence: The manuscript presents fluorescence microscopy data on presynaptic markers.

claim: Increased calcium influx can recruit more synaptic vesicles to release sites.
source: consistent with the notion that increased calcium influx can recruit more synaptic vesicles to release sites (Thanawala and Regehr, 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study to support the interpretation of the data.

claim: There is a marked increase in the size of UNC-29::GFP clusters in unc-2(zf35gf) mutants.
source: Importantly, we also observed a marked increase in the size of UNC-29::GFP clusters, indicating a concomitant increase in the postsynaptic receptors (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: The manuscript presents fluorescence microscopy data on postsynaptic markers.

claim: unc-2(zf35gf) mutants are hypersensitive to levamisole.
source: unc-2(zf35gf) mutants were hypersensitive to levamisole, consistent with an increased AChR expression on the muscle cell membrane (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents pharmacological assay data.

claim: Hypersensitivity to levamisole is consistent with increased AChR expression on the muscle cell membrane.
source: unc-2(zf35gf) mutants were hypersensitive to levamisole, consistent with an increased AChR expression on the muscle cell membrane (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript interprets the levamisole sensitivity data.

claim: In unc-2(zf35gf) mutants, RAB-3::mCherry puncta at GABAergic NMJs are enlarged to a level comparable to that observed for cholinergic NMJs.
source: In unc-2(zf35gf) mutants, RAB-3::mCherry puncta were enlarged, to a level comparable to that observed for cholinergic NMJs (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: The manuscript presents fluorescence microscopy data comparing presynaptic markers at different synapse types.

claim: UNC-49::GFP puncta are severely reduced in both size and number in unc-2(zf35gf) mutants.
source: However, UNC-49::GFP puncta were severely reduced in both size and number (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: The manuscript presents fluorescence microscopy data on GABAergic postsynaptic markers.

claim: In unc-2(zf35gf) mutants, RAB-3::mCherry puncta density is slightly increased.
source: In unc-2(zf35gf) mutants, RAB-3::mCherry puncta density was slightly increased, whereas UNC-49::GFP puncta density was reduced compared to wild type (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative analysis of puncta density.

claim: UNC-49::GFP puncta density is reduced in unc-2(zf35gf) mutants compared to wild type.
source: In unc-2(zf35gf) mutants, RAB-3::mCherry puncta density was slightly increased, whereas UNC-49::GFP puncta density was reduced compared to wild type (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative analysis of puncta density.

claim: At some NMJs in unc-2(zf35gf) mutants, RAB-3::mCherry puncta are present without punctate UNC-49::GFP apposition.
source: At some NMJs, we noted the presence of RAB-3::mCherry puncta without punctate UNC-49::GFP apposition (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), suggesting post-synaptic silencing of GABA synapses.
evidence: The manuscript presents microscopy observations and interprets them.

claim: RNA-seq experiments show no obvious changes in unc-49 and unc-29 expression levels in wild-type vs unc-2(zf35gf) animals.
source: RNA-seq experiments showed no obvious changes in the unc-49 and unc-29 expression level in wild-type vs unc-2(zf35gf) animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 4)
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-seq data.

claim: The morphological changes in UNC-49::GFP and UNC-29::GFP fluorescence signals suggest post-transcriptional changes in receptor localization and distribution.
source: suggesting post-transcriptional changes in UNC-49 and UNC-29 receptor localization and distribution.
evidence: The manuscript infers post-transcriptional regulation from the combined RNA-seq and microscopy data.

claim: unc-2(zf35gf) mutants exhibit reduced sensitivity to muscimol.
source: unc-2(zf35gf) mutants exhibited reduced sensitivity to muscimol: most unc-2(zf35gf) mutants were able to generate backward locomotion upon the head touch (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript presents pharmacological assay data.

claim: Partial resistance to muscimol-induced muscle relaxation is consistent with reduction of UNC-49/GABAA expression at the muscle cell surface.
source: The partial resistance of unc-2(zf35gf) mutants to muscimol-induced muscle relaxation is consistent with reduction of UNC-49/GABAA expression at the muscle cell surface.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the muscimol sensitivity data.

claim: Unchanged spontaneous EPSC and IPSC amplitudes suggest that the density of functional cholinergic and GABAergic receptors at individual synapses is unchanged in unc-2(zf35gf) mutants.
source: However, both spontaneous EPSC and IPSC amplitudes are not significantly different between unc-2(zf35gf) mutants and the wild type. This suggests that the density of functional cholinergic and GABAergic receptors at individual synapses is unchanged in unc-2(zf35gf) mutants.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the electrophysiological data.

claim: The synaptic fluorescence changes most likely indicate increases or decreases in the number of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic connections.
source: As individual synapses can be difficult to resolve with confocal microscopy, single fluorescent puncta often represent multiple synapses. Therefore, the synaptic fluorescence changes we observe most likely indicate increases or decreases in the number of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic connections.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the microscopy data considering technical limitations.

claim: Expression of unc-2(zf35gf) in GABAergic motor neurons alone results in an increase in both presynaptic RAB-3::mCherry and post-synaptic UNC-49::GFP fluorescence.
source: Expression in GABAergic motor neurons alone resulted in an increase in both presynaptic RAB-3::mCherry and post-synaptic UNC-49::GFP fluorescence (Figure 7A and B; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents cell-specific expression experiments.

claim: Punc-47::UNC-2(GF) animals are partially resistant to aldicarb, indicative of increased GABAergic signaling onto body wall muscles.
source: Punc-47::UNC-2(GF) animals are partially resistant to aldicarb, indicative of increased GABAergic signaling onto the body wall muscles (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents pharmacological data on cell-specific transgenic animals.

claim: The reduction of GABAergic synapses in unc-2(zf35gf) mutants is not a direct consequence of elevated GABAergic neuron activity.
source: Thus, the reduction of GABAergic synapses in unc-2(zf35gf) mutants is not a direct consequence of elevated GABAergic neuron activity.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the cell-specific expression experiments.

claim: Increased GABAergic motor neuron activity in principle leads to increases in both presynaptic and postsynaptic termini similar to that observed for cholinergic synapses.
source: Instead, our results indicate that increased GABAergic motor neuron activity in principle leads to increases in both presynaptic and postsynaptic termini similar to that observed for cholinergic synapses.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the cell-specific expression experiments.

claim: Expression of unc-2(zf35gf) only in cholinergic neurons reduces UNC-49::GFP fluorescence to a similar degree as in unc-2(zf35gf) mutants.
source: Indeed, when we expressed unc-2(zf35gf) only in cholinergic neurons (Pacr-2::UNC-2(GF)), UNC-49::GFP fluorescence was reduced to a similar degree as in the unc-2(zf35gf) mutants (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: The manuscript presents cell-specific expression experiments.

claim: Presynaptic RAB-3::mCherry fluorescence in GABAergic neurons is slightly increased in Pacr-2::UNC-2(GF) animals.
source: Presynaptic RAB-3::mCherry fluorescence in GABAergic neurons was slightly increased in Pacr-2::UNC-2(GF) animals (Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The manuscript presents microscopy data on cell-specific transgenic animals.

claim: Increased presynaptic RAB-3::mCherry in GABAergic neurons of Pacr-2::UNC-2(GF) animals may reflect increased stimulation of GABAergic motor neurons by cholinergic motor neurons.
source: which may reflect increased stimulation of GABAergic motor neurons by cholinergic motor neurons.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the microscopy data.

claim: Expression of unc-2(zf35gf) in cholinergic motor neurons increases sensitivity to aldicarb.
source: Expression of an unc-2(zf35gf) transgene in cholinergic motor neurons increased sensitivity to aldicarb, consistent with an expected increase in cholinergic signaling (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents pharmacological data on cell-specific transgenic animals.

claim: Increased activity of cholinergic motor neurons in unc-2(zf35gf) mutants is required and causes the decrease in GABAergic synapses.
source: Together, these results suggest that increased activity of cholinergic motor neurons in unc-2(zf35gf) mutants is not only required but also causes the decrease in GABAergic synapses.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the cell-specific expression experiments.

claim: In both unc-2(zf35gf); acr-12 and unc-2(zf35gf); unc-29 mutants, UNC-49::GFP fluorescence is restored to wild-type levels.
source: In both unc-2(zf35gf); acr-12 and unc-2(zf35gf); unc-29 mutants, UNC-49::GFP fluorescence was restored to wild-type levels (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: The manuscript presents genetic interaction experiments.

claim: Increased cholinergic input to body wall muscles is the primary signal for decreasing the number of GABA synapses.
source: This finding indicates that increased cholinergic input to body wall muscles is the primary signal for decreasing the number of GABA synapses.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the genetic interaction experiments.

claim: GABA signaling is not required for UNC-49/GABAAR expression or localization in body wall muscles.
source: However, GABA signaling is not required for UNC-49/GABAAR expression or localization in body wall muscles (Gally and Bessereau, 2003).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study.

claim: Increased cholinergic input to body wall muscles negatively regulates GABAergic postsynapse formation or stability.
source: Together, these results suggest that increased cholinergic input to body wall muscles negatively regulates GABAergic postsynapse formation or stability.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the genetic interaction experiments.

claim: Muscle-specific expression of hyperactive levamisole-sensitive AChR (L-AChR(GF)) leads to increased excitation of body wall muscles but no obvious defects in muscle structure or cholinergic synapses.
source: Muscle-specific expression of the hyperactive levamisole-sensitive AChR (L-AChR(GF)) containing gain-of-function mutations in L-AChR subunits UNC-29 and UNC-38, leads to increased excitation of body wall muscles, but no obvious defects in muscle structure or cholinergic synapses (Bhattacharya et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study describing the L-AChR(GF) transgenic animals.

claim: L-AChR(gf) transgenic animals exhibit normal presynaptic marker expression at GABAergic NMJs.
source: L-AChR(gf) transgenic animals exhibited normal presynaptic marker expression at GABAergic NMJs.
evidence: The manuscript presents microscopy data on L-AChR(gf) animals.

claim: Postsynaptic UNC-49::GFP fluorescence is markedly reduced in L-AChR(gf) animals.
source: However, similar to unc-2(zf35gf) mutants, postsynaptic UNC-49::GFP fluorescence was markedly reduced in L-AChR(gf) animals (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: The manuscript presents microscopy data on L-AChR(gf) animals.

claim: Transgenic expression of wild-type L-AChR does not affect UNC-49::GFP fluorescence.
source: Transgenic expression of the wild-type L-AChR (Pmyo-3::L-AChR(wt)) did not affect UNC-49::GFP fluorescence.
evidence: The manuscript presents control experiments with wild-type L-AChR.

claim: Increased cholinergic signaling onto muscles in unc-2(zf35gf) mutants negatively regulates GABAergic postsynapse formation.
source: This indicates that increased cholinergic signaling onto muscles in unc-2(zf35gf) mutants negatively regulates GABAergic postsynapse formation.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the L-AChR experiments.

claim: Sustained high Ca2+ levels reduce inhibitory synaptic strength through a calcineurin-dependent lateral diffusion of GABAA receptor from synapses in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: In particular, sustained high Ca2+ levels reduce inhibitory synaptic strength through a calcineurin-dependent lateral diffusion of GABAA receptor from synapses (Bannai et al., 2009; Bannai et al., 2015; Muir et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on calcineurin-dependent regulation of GABAA receptors.

claim: UNC-49::GFP expression is not significantly different in tax-6(lf) mutants.
source: UNC-49::GFP expression was not significantly different in tax-6(lf) mutants (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: The manuscript presents microscopy data on tax-6 mutants.

claim: The tax-6(lf) mutation restores UNC-49::GFP fluorescence in unc-2(zf35gf) mutants.
source: However, the tax-6(lf) mutation restored UNC-49::GFP fluorescence in unc-2(zf35gf) mutants.
evidence: The manuscript presents genetic interaction experiments with tax-6.

claim: tax-6 RNAi feeding restores UNC-49::GFP fluorescence in unc-2(zf35gf) mutants.
source: tax-6 RNAi feeding restored UNC-49::GFP fluorescence in unc-2(zf35gf) mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 3)
evidence: The manuscript presents RNAi experiments.

claim: TAX-6 acts in muscle to regulate GABA synapses.
source: suggesting that TAX-6 acts in muscle to regulate GABA synapses.
evidence: The manuscript infers the site of TAX-6 action from RNAi experiments.

claim: Increased cholinergic input to body wall muscles reduces the number of GABAergic postsynapses in a calcineurin-dependent manner.
source: Together, these results indicate that increased cholinergic input to body wall muscles reduces the number of GABAergic postsynapses in a calcineurin-dependent manner.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the tax-6 experiments.

claim: unc-2(zf35gf) mutants are hyperactive and exhibit seizure-like motor behaviors, in contrast to the sluggish behavior of unc-2(lf) mutants.
source: unc-2(zf35gf) mutants are hyperactive and exhibit seizure-like motor behaviors, in contrast to the sluggish behavior of unc-2(lf) mutants (Schafer and Kenyon, 1995; Mathews et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript compares the phenotypes of gain-of-function and loss-of-function mutants and cites previous studies.

claim: The unc-2(zf35gf) mutation results in a G-to-R substitution in a highly conserved region in the intracellular linker between TMIII and TMIV.
source: The unc-2(zf35gf) mutation results in a G-to-R substitution in a highly conserved region in the intracellular linker between TMIII and TMIV.
evidence: The manuscript describes the location and conservation of the mutation.

claim: The G-to-R substitution causes a shift to lower voltages of activation and reduced inactivation of the channel to increase Ca2+ influx.
source: Our electrophysiological analyses of the human CACNA1A channel in HEK cells indicate that this G-to-R substitution causes a shift to lower voltages of activation and reduced inactivation of the channel to increase Ca2+ influx.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the electrophysiological findings.

claim: A similar G-to-R substitution in an intracellular linker of the human CaV1.2 channel results in similar defects in channel inactivation that underlies Timothy syndrome.
source: A similar G-to-R substitution in an intracellular linker of the human CaV1.2 channel results in similar defects in channel inactivation that underlies Timothy syndrome (Splawski et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study on a related channel mutation.

claim: The negative shift in the activation potential of UNC-2/CaV2α(GF) channel is reminiscent of similar observations for several mutant human CaV2.1α channels identified in FHM1 patients.
source: The negative shift in the activation potential of UNC-2/CaV2α(GF) channel is reminiscent of similar observations for several mutant human CaV2.1α channels that have been identified in patients with familial hemiplegic migraine type 1 (FHM1) (Hans et al., 1999; Tottene et al., 2005; Müllner et al., 2004).

claim: Most FHM1 mutations appear to lead to channel activation at lower voltages and/or increased channel open probability.
